name: End-of-history illusion
statement: People of every age report having changed a lot over the past decade and expect to change little over the next one.
meaning: The claim has two halves that only look consistent from inside. Asked how much their personality, values or tastes shifted over the last ten years, people report a lot. Asked how much those things will shift over the next ten, the same sort of people report a little. Since everyone was once ten years younger, both answers cannot be right, and the label treats the forward-looking one as the mistake. That is a claim about prediction rather than about memory. It predicts something testable, which is that a person's forecast of their future self should fall short of what that person later turns out to be.

origin.who: Jordi Quoidbach, Daniel T. Gilbert and Timothy D. Wilson
origin.note: Their design compared predictors aged a with reporters aged a + 10, drawn from the same recruitment pool. No participant was measured twice, so the ten-year gap in the analysis is a gap between people rather than a gap in anyone's life.

evidence: Six studies. In study 1, 7,519 adults aged 18 to 68 completed the Ten Item Personality Inventory, then rated themselves either as they had been ten years earlier or as they expected to be ten years later. The condition coefficient was b = -0.14, p < 0.001. Study 2 ran the same design on 2,717 adults using ten values from the Schwartz Value Inventory, b = -0.46. Study 3 asked 7,130 adults about five concrete preferences, including favourite band and best friend, b = -0.19. A follow-up on 613 adults put each person in both conditions and gave b = -7.69, p = 0.001. To test whether reporters were simply misremembering, the authors set their intraclass correlations against 3,808 adults measured twice in the MacArthur Midlife Development survey: 0.52 for actual change, 0.51 for reported change, 0.65 for predicted change. Study 4 recruited 170 people on Mechanical Turk, who said they would pay $129 to see their current favourite band in ten years and $80 to see their ten-years-ago favourite band next week, 61% more for the future concert.

replication.headline: The one longitudinal test produced two papers reading the same data in opposite directions, and the disagreement is about whether change is counted with its sign.
replication.detail: Harris and Busseri tested the claim on life satisfaction across three waves of the MacArthur Midlife Development survey, which records both what people predicted and what later happened. They concluded that most individuals were accurate or expected too much change rather than too little. Quoidbach, Gilbert and Wilson re-analysed the same survey and concluded the opposite, reporting that predicted absolute change fell short of experienced absolute change, b = 0.15, t(10,430) = 8.46, p < 0.001, over 3,909 participants and 14,174 observations. Busseri and Harris then reproduced that result in their own 2,390-person subsample, b = 0.16, t(2,389) = 5.51, p < 0.001, with mean experienced change of 0.97 against mean predicted change of 0.82. They located the disagreement in the measure. Counted as absolute values the effect appears, yet only 36% of individuals predicted too little change, while 38% were accurate and 26% predicted too much. Counted with direction kept, b = 0.26, t(2,389) = 7.13, p < 0.001, and people in their thirties, forties and fifties expected too much improvement while those in their seventies expected too much decline. The pattern itself reappears in other cross-sectional designs. Children aged 4 to 11 show it within subjects (N = 256) but not when asked about other people (N = 83), public service professionals randomised to report or predict show it for work motivations, and it is larger among US Americans than among Japanese.

study.cite: Harris, H., & Busseri, M. A. (2019). Is there an 'end of history illusion' for life satisfaction? Evidence from a three-wave longitudinal study. Journal of Research in Personality, 83, 103869.

limits: The 2013 design is cross-sectional and the claim is developmental. A 33-year-old's forecast was set against a 43-year-old's recollection, so cohort differences and errors of prediction cannot be separated. The paper states no such caveat. In their 2020 comment the same three authors list their own 2013 studies among work 'limited by the use of retrospective or peer-reports rather than directly measuring change'. The only limitation the 2013 supplement raises is that too few older participants took part to say whether the illusion survives at the top of the age range. Over 80% of participants in studies 1 to 3 were women, recruited through the website of a French television programme. The MacArthur comparison used a different scale from the authors' own, and they say direct comparison of the data was not possible. All the longitudinal work covers life satisfaction on a single-item scale, not personality, values or preferences, and Busseri and Harris record that their analyses were not preregistered. No preregistered replication of the 2013 protocol was found: PubMed returns eight records for the phrase, Crossref none beyond this exchange and its extensions, and Science carries no technical comment on the paper.
misreadings: The 2013 studies cannot show that anybody was wrong about the future, because no future was measured. They show that forecasts collected at one age are smaller than recollections collected at another. The nearest thing to an accuracy test in the paper compares two different samples on two different scales, which is why the authors report intraclass correlations rather than a difference. The 19,000 figure covers six studies; the largest single sample is 7,519 and the concert result rests on 170 people. The finding is also not that people expect to stop changing. Predicted change was smaller than reported change, not zero. And the version of the claim that survives longitudinal data is about absolute magnitude. Restore the sign and the same records show younger adults expecting too much improvement, which is the opposite error from expecting too little change.
